growth_story.headline: Albania's income per person collapsed after communism, boomed on remittances to 2008, slowed, then climbed on tourism to a record high in 2025.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 income per person shrank 1.9 percent a year on average. It fell 27.6 percent in 1991 as the communist economy broke down, grew fast from 1993 to 1996, then fell sharply again in 1997 when pyramid schemes collapsed and unrest halted production. From 1998 to 2008 growth averaged 7.6 percent a year, the fastest era; the World Bank links it to construction and services, and to consumption paid for by remittances from Albanians abroad, wages and strong growth in credit. From 2009 to 2025 growth slowed to 4.4 percent a year: the 2008 global crisis cut remittances and credit, and income per person grew only 2.7 percent in 2011 and 2.6 percent in 2012. Growth then picked up to 5.1 percent a year over 2016–2025, up from 4.5 over 2006–2015; after a dip in 2020 with the 2019 earthquake and the pandemic, income per person rebounded 10.7 percent in 2021, and the IMF credits tourism for lifting output well above its pre-pandemic trend. Income per person reached a new high in 2025, while the IMF and World Bank point to emigration, an ageing population and weak productivity as forces slowing convergence with the European Union.

threads.title: Collapse and pyramid schemes
threads.text: Albania began its move to a market economy in 1991 in deep poverty, and income per person fell 27.6 percent that year. After fast growth from 1993 to 1996, huge pyramid investment schemes collapsed in 1997, setting off riots and the fall of the government, and output fell as production stopped during the disorder.

threads.text: From 1998 to 2008 income per person grew 7.6 percent a year. The World Bank finds that construction and services led output, while consumption was paid for by remittances from Albanians working abroad, by wages and by strong growth in credit.

threads.title: The 2008 shock
threads.text: After 2008 the global crisis cut remittances from Albanians abroad, and banks cut the supply of credit. The World Bank says the shock exposed a growth model that relied on money from abroad to pay for consumption; income per person grew only 2.7 percent in 2011 and 2.6 percent in 2012.

threads.title: Tourism after the pandemic
threads.text: An earthquake in November 2019 and the pandemic brought a dip in 2020, then income per person rebounded 10.7 percent in 2021. Since then a tourism boom and private consumption have driven growth, and the IMF says tourism has carried output well above its pre-pandemic trend.

threads.text: Emigration and an ageing population weigh on the number of workers, and the IMF finds that output per hour worked has barely improved in a decade. Income per person is still far below the European Union average.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes steady output growth in 2022–2024, yet income per person rose faster, by 6.5, 5.7 and 5.6 percent in those years. Income per person can grow faster than output only when the number of people falls, and the World Bank and IMF point to outmigration, an ageing population and a shrinking working-age population, so part of the climb to a record level in 2025 reflects fewer people rather than faster output alone.
